subtitle: The cheapest bug to fix is the one caught before any code: get the right thing specified.

kinds.body:
Imagine ordering a car. “It must have four wheels and an engine” is one kind of requirement; “it must be fast and safe” is another, and the second kind is where the arguments start. Functional requirements say what the system does (“a user can reset a password by email”). Non-functional requirements constrain how well: performance, security, usability, availability, portability.

Here is the rule that saves projects: a good requirement is testable. Write “responds in under 2 s for 95 % of requests”, not “fast”. Can you test “fast”? No. So “the site must handle 1000 users at once” is a non-functional requirement, and a testable one.
keynotes: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional requirements constrain how: performance, security, usability, availability, portability.
A good requirement is testable: “responds in under 2 s for 95 % of requests”, not “fast”.
“The site must handle 1000 users at once” is a non-functional requirement.

elic.body:
Where do requirements come from? From people, and people rarely say what they mean on the first try. So you dig: interviews, questionnaires, observation, workshops, prototypes, and studying existing documents. And stakeholders disagree, so requirements must be negotiated and prioritised (e.g. MoSCoW: must, should, could, won’t).

The loop in the figure is elicit, draft, review, baseline, and you may go round it several times. In MoSCoW, “won’t” means not this time: it is agreed to be out of scope for now, not forgotten.
keynotes: Elicitation techniques: interviews, questionnaires, observation, workshops, prototypes and studying existing documents.
Stakeholders disagree, so requirements must be negotiated and prioritised, for example with MoSCoW: must, should, could, won’t.
The loop is elicit, draft, review, baseline.

story.body:
How do you write down behaviour so that both customers and developers understand it? Two popular ways. A use case describes an actor achieving a goal in steps, with alternate flows for failures. A user story fits on a sticky note: “As a role I want goal so that benefit”, with acceptance criteria. Stories are small and estimated in points.

A good user story ends with its benefit, the “so that…”, because that tells you why the feature matters. The use case in the figure appears as a card, step by step.
keynotes: A use case describes an actor achieving a goal in steps, with alternate flows for failures.
A user story reads “As a role I want goal so that benefit”, with acceptance criteria; stories are small and estimated in points.
A good user story ends with its benefit.

srs.body:
At some point the requirements need a home, and you will write it, a document everyone can point to. That is the Software Requirements Specification (IEEE 830/29148). It contains an introduction (purpose, scope, definitions), an overall description (users, constraints), specific requirements (functional, external interfaces, performance, design constraints), and appendices.

A good SRS is complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable. Spot the ambiguous one for yourself: “the system shall be user-friendly” is ambiguous, because two readers will picture two different things.
keynotes: The SRS (IEEE 830/29148) has an introduction, an overall description, specific requirements and appendices.
Specific requirements cover functional needs, external interfaces, performance and design constraints.
It must be complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable.

valid.body:
Requirements are never finished, because the world keeps changing. You validate them by reviews, prototypes and test-case writing. And when they change, which they will, you manage change with a recorded process: request → impact analysis → approval → update and trace. Traceability links each requirement to design, code and tests.

Measure the churn. A project has 120 requirements; 24 change after baseline. Volatility = 24/120 = 20%. High volatility suggests the requirements were poorly understood, or the business is unstable, so you should expect risk.
keynotes: Validate requirements by reviews, prototypes and test-case writing.
Manage change with a recorded process: request, impact analysis, approval, update and trace; traceability links each requirement to design, code and tests.
24 changes out of 120 requirements is a volatility of 20%.

fp.body:
How big is a project, before you have written a single line of code? Counting lines is impossible, so function points count what the user can see: external inputs (EI), outputs (EO), inquiries (EQ), internal files (ILF) and external interfaces (EIF), each weighted by complexity. Unadjusted FP = Σ count × weight; multiply by a value adjustment factor (0.65–1.35).

Work it out with average weights EI 4, EO 5, EQ 4, ILF 10, EIF 7 and counts EI 10, EO 6, EQ 5, ILF 4, EIF 2. UFP = 40 + 30 + 20 + 40 + 14 = 144. Function points are useful because they measure size from the requirements, independent of programming language.
keynotes: Function points count user-visible functions: external inputs, outputs, inquiries, internal files and external interfaces, each weighted by complexity.
Unadjusted FP = Σ count × weight; multiply by a value adjustment factor (0.65–1.35).
With the average weights and the given counts, UFP = 40 + 30 + 20 + 40 + 14 = 144.
